statement.text:
A word in an alphabet A = {a , a , . . . , a } is called a palindrome if it reads
                                           1   2        n
the same from left to right and from right to left. Let k a non-negative integer.
A word in the alphabet A is called an almost k-palindrome if it can be transformed
into a palindrome by changing ⩽ k letters in it. (So an almost 0-palindrome is a
palindrome.) Let elements of a free group F2 = ⟨x, y⟩ be represented as words in the
alphabet {x±1 , y ±1 }. Do there exist positive integers m and c such that every element
in F2 is a product of ⩽ c almost m-palindromes?
    It is known that for m = 0 there is no such a number c.              V. G. Bardakov
  ∗ No, there are no such integers (M. Staiger, J. Algebra, 659 (2024), 475–481).
